s.d: the residue from a burned substance{N:001}
s.c: It may be important in rendering σποδὸς δαμάλεως to indicate that the ashes are the result of the animal having been burned as a sacrifice, for example, ‘the ashes of a heifer burned as a sacrifice.’ Otherwise, the relationship between ‘ashes’ and ‘heifer’ may be difficult, if not impossible, for readers to understand.

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of σπορά ‘sowing of seed,’ not occurring in the NT) the instrumental means of birth
(derivative of {L:σπείρω<SDBG:σπείρω:000000>} ‘to sow,’ {D:43.6}) grain growing in a field
s.c: In a number of languages there are distinct terms for various stages of growth of grain, and in view of the context of the account in ⟦Mark 2:23|Mark 2:23⟧ and parallel passages, it is important to indicate that the grain was essentially ripe.

s.d: the kernel part of fruit, usually grain
s.c: A number of languages make distinctions between two quite different types of seed: (1) those produced by grasses (that is to say, grains) and (2) those produced by other types of plants, for example, beans, squash, apples, etc. In all passages employing the Greek terms in this subdomain (κόκκος, σπέρμα, σπόρος), it is best to use some expression referring to ‘grain.’|See also LN 10.23 for σπορά ‘seed’ used figuratively of descendants.

s.d: to do something hurriedly, with the implication of associated energy{N:001}
s.g: to hasten to; to hurry to; to do quickly

s.d: to do something with intense effort and motivation
s.g: to work hard; to do one’s best; to endeavor

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
s.d: to be eager to do something, with the implication of readiness to expend energy and effort

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
s.d: pertaining to being earnest and diligent in undertaking an activity
s.c: In a number of languages eagerness can only be expressed in terms of desire. Hence, for ⟦Philippians 2:28|Philippians 2:28⟧ one must sometimes translate ‘I am all the more desirous of sending him to you.”

s.d: (derivative of {L:σπουδή<SDBG:σπουδή:000001>}[b] ‘to endeavor,’ {D:68.63}) pertaining to intense effort in accomplishing some goal
s.g: making an effort to; doing one’s best

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
s.d: pertaining to being earnest and diligent in undertaking an activity
s.c: In a number of languages eagerness can only be expressed in terms of desire. Hence, for ⟦Philippians 2:28|Philippians 2:28⟧ one must sometimes translate ‘I am all the more desirous of sending him to you.”

s.d: to do something hurriedly, with the implication of associated energy{N:001}
s.g: to hasten to; to hurry to; to do quickly

s.d: to do something with intense effort and motivation
s.g: to work hard; to do one’s best; to endeavor

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
s.d: to be eager to do something, with the implication of readiness to expend energy and effort
(an idiom, literally: to bring every effort to) to do one’s very best in attempting to do something
s.g: to do one’s best; to make every effort to; to try as hard as possible
s.c: In some languages it may be almost impossible to speak of ‘adding goodness to faith’ (⟦2 Peter 1:5|2 Peter 1:5⟧). However, an appropriate equivalent of this expression may be ‘do your best to be good as well as to believe.’

s.d: a basket which is presumably somewhat larger than a {L:κόφινος<SDBG:κόφινος:000000>} ({D:6.150}){N:001}
an open, oval area (frequently including a racetrack) around which was built an enclosed series of tiers of seats for those who came to watch the spectacles
s.c: In ⟦1 Corinthians 9:24|1 Corinthians 9:24⟧ the important feature is not the stadium as a construction, but as a place where races were conducted. Accordingly, ‘all the runners in the stadium’ may very well be rendered as ‘all the runners who are racing.’ The focus here is upon the competition rather than upon the type of place in which the competition took place.

s.d: a jar regularly used for wine, but in the NT it refers to the jar in which manna was kept permanently
act of rising up in open defiance of authority, with the presumed intention to overthrow it or to act in complete opposition to its demands{N:001}
to engage in intense and emotional expressions of different opinions
the state of existence, with the implication of being in a place or position
a silver coin worth two didrachma or approximately four denarii

s.dp: Artifacts › Instruments Used in Punishment and Execution
s.d: a pole stuck into the ground in an upright position with a crosspiece attached to its upper part; used as a means of execution
s.c: In ⟦Matthew 27:32|Matthew 27:32⟧ (τοῦτον ἠγγάρευσαν ἵνα ἄρῃ τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ ‘they forced him to carry Jesus’ cross’) the reference is probably to the crosspiece of the cross, which normally would have been carried by a man condemned to die.|Because of the symbolism associated with the cross, translations of the NT in all languages preserve some expression which will identify the cross, not only as a means of capital punishment, but as having a particular form, namely, an upright pole with a crossbeam. In some receptor languages the term for a cross means simply ‘crossbeam.’ In other instances it is composed of a phrase meaning ‘crossed poles.’ It is important, however, to avoid an expression which will suggest crossed sticks in the form of X rather than a cross consisting of an upright with a horizontal beam. If at all possible one should employ a term or phrase which may be used in an extended sense, since in so many contexts the term ‘cross’ refers not only to the instrument of Christ’s death, but to the event of execution. It also becomes a symbol of the message of forgiveness and of reconciliation. Because of these extended meanings, it is important to choose a form which can, if at all possible, support these additional meanings.

s.d: to execute someone by nailing that person to a cross
s.c: It is rare that one can find in receptor languages a technical term or phrase meaning specifically ‘to crucify.’ In general, a phrase must be employed, since this type of execution is no longer practiced. One can, for example, use such expressions as ‘to nail to a cross bar’ or ‘to nail up on wood’ or even ‘to nail up high.’

s.d: the small round fruit, sweet and juicy, of a creeping plant that develops a woody stem when it matures; Vitis vinifera; symbol of blessing, prosperity, and happiness
s.c: Some scholars have contended that βότρυς means primarily a bunch of grapes, while σταφυλή designates individual grapes. In ⟦Revelation 14:18|Revelation 14:18⟧ this difference might seem plausible, but there is scarcely any evidence for such a distinction, since both words may signify grapes as well as bunches of grapes.|In some languages it is necessary to borrow a term for ‘grapes’ from a dominant language and then employ some kind of classifier, for example, ‘fruit called grapes.’ In other languages grapes may be known as ‘wine fruit,’ since wine may be more widely known than a term for grapes.

s.d: the dense spiky cluster in which the seeds of grain such as wheat and barley grow (restricted in NT contexts to references to wheat)
s.g: ear of wheat; head of wheat
s.c: In some languages it is impossible to speak of ‘a head of wheat’ or ‘an ear of wheat,’ since terms referring to ‘head’ and ‘ear’ have no such figurative extensions of meaning. In certain instances the equivalent may be ‘the point of the wheat’ or ‘the brush of the wheat,’ referring to the spike-like objects which extend from each grain.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person greeted in {S:04501600900018}

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: the area on the top of a flat-roof house
s.c: In general, the types of roofs referred to in the NT are flat-top, made of pounded dirt, sometimes mixed with lime or stone, and supported by heavy beams. In view of the various types of activities described as taking place on the housetop, it may be important in some languages to indicate either in the text or in a marginal note the fact that such housetops were flat and that there was usually easy access to such roofs.

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Patience, Endurance, Perseverance
s.d: to put up with annoyance or difficulty
s.g: to put up with; to endure

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Birth, Procreation
s.d: the state of not being able to conceive and bear children
s.g: barren; not able to bear children

s.d: to keep oneself away from some activity
purposely to avoid association with someone{N:001}
s.g: to shun; to avoid; to keep away from; to have nothing to do with

s.d: a wreath of wool to which leaves and flowers might be added and either wound around a staff or woven into a garland to be worn on the head
s.c: Garlands were an important part of the ritual involved in the worship of pagan gods in the ancient world. Such a garland may be described as ‘a circle of leaves’ or ‘a ring of flowers’ or ‘a wreath of flowers.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Laugh, Cry, Groan
s.d: groaning or sighing as the result of deep concern or stress
s.c: To groan or to sigh may be the result of quite different circumstances, and in a number of languages a clear distinction must be made in any term for groaning or sighing, depending upon the reason or basis for such an expression of emotion. In ⟦Mark 7:34|Mark 7:34⟧ the sigh or groan would seem to be an expression of sympathy for the deaf-mute, but in ⟦Acts 7:34|Acts 7:34⟧ the groans would be caused by severe misery and oppression.

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Laugh, Cry, Groan
s.d: to groan or sigh as the result of deep concern or stress
s.g: to groan; to sigh; groan; sigh
s.c: To groan or to sigh may be the result of quite different circumstances, and in a number of languages a clear distinction must be made in any term for groaning or sighing, depending upon the reason or basis for such an expression of emotion. In ⟦Mark 7:34|Mark 7:34⟧ the sigh or groan would seem to be an expression of sympathy for the deaf-mute, but in ⟦Mark 7:34|Mark 7:34⟧ the groans would be caused by severe misery and oppression.

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:στενάζω<SDBG:στενάζω:000000>}[a] ‘to groan, to sigh,’ {D:25.143}) to complain in an intensive and excessive manner
s.c: It may even be possible to retain something of the figurative meaning of στενάζω in ⟦James 5:9|James 5:9⟧ by translating ‘do not complain with moaning’ or ‘do not moan and complain against.’

s.d: pertaining to being narrow or restricted
to be under severe limitations or restrictions
s.g: to live under restrictions; to be restricted; to be confined
s.c: In a number of languages it may be more meaningful to render ⟦2 Corinthians 6:12|2 Corinthians 6:12⟧ as ‘it is not that we impose restrictions on you; it is you yourselves who are doing it.’ For another interpretation of στενοχωρέομαι in ⟦2 Corinthians 6:12|2 Corinthians 6:12⟧ as part of an idiom, see LN 25.54.

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Experience Trouble, Hardship
s.d: to be in serious circumstances, with the implication of no escape or way out
s.g: to be in great trouble; to be hemmed in with difficulty

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Love, Affection, Compassion
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to be restricted in the bowels) to restrict one’s affection for someone
s.g: to not respond with affection to someone; to close one’s heart to
s.c: In ⟦2 Corinthians 6:12|2 Corinthians 6:12⟧ it is also possible to understand στενοχωρέομαι as meaning ‘to live with severe restrictions’ (see LN 37.18), and σπλάγχνα may be interpreted as a psychological faculty of intent and feeling (see LN 26.11).

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Trouble, Hardship, Distress
s.d: a set of difficult circumstances, implying certain restrictions
s.c: ‘Distress’ may be expressed in some languages as ‘people will be in trouble’ or in an idiomatic expression, ‘the world will fall on people.’

s.d: pertaining to being solid or firm in contrast with that which is soft or liquid
pertaining to being firm and steadfast in one’s attitudes or beliefs
s.g: to be firm; to be strong

s.d: to make physically strong
s.c: In a number of languages one cannot speak of a name doing anything or even the ‘power of a name’ accomplishing some goal. Since in Greek the use of ὄνομα ‘name’ is essentially a metonym for the person, it is often necessary to translate an expression such as is in ⟦Acts 3:16|Acts 3:16⟧ as ‘Christ made him strong’ or ‘Jesus made him strong.’ Such an expression, however, should not imply that this was a miracle performed directly by Jesus, either before or immediately after the resurrection.

s.d: to cause someone to become stronger in the sense of more firm and unchanging in attitude or belief
s.g: to strengthen; to make more firm

s.d: to be physically strong and vigorous
s.g: to be strong; to become strong

s.d: a state of firm, inner strength
s.g: firm position; being firm in; firmness; steadfastness

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Christian of Corinth
a wreath consisting either of foliage or of precious metals formed to resemble foliage and worn as a symbol of honor, victory, or as a badge of high office
s.c: It may be important in some contexts to indicate clearly the significance of the wreath worn on the head, for example, ‘a wreath to show victory.’ To describe ‘a wreath’ merely as ‘a circle of leaves’ would hardly be sufficient to indicate its cultural significance. In order to do justice to the cultural relevance of such a wreath, it may be important to add some type of marginal note (compare διάδημα ‘diadem crown,’ LN 6.196).

s.d: a prize or reward given as the result of outstanding performance
s.c: In ⟦Revelation 2:10|Revelation 2:10⟧ the relationship between τὸν στέφανον and τῆς ζωῆς is one of apposition, for the prize consists of life. Essentially the same relationship exists in the construction ἀπόκειταί μοι ὁ τῆς δικαιοσύνης στέφανος ‘the prize of righteousness awaits me’ ⟦2 Timothy 4:8|2 Timothy 4:8⟧. In this case the prize is ‘being declared righteous’ or ‘being put right with God.’

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:στέφανος<SDBG:στέφανος:000000>}[a] ‘wreath, crown,’ {D:6.192}) a symbol of successful activity
s.g: crown; symbol of success; sign of accomplishment

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: one of the seven helpers in the church in Jerusalem and the first Christian martyr
(derivative of {L:στέφανος<SDBG:στέφανος:000001>}[b] ‘prize, reward,’ {D:57.121}) to cause someone to receive a prize or reward as the result of excellence in competition
s.g: to give a prize; to provide a reward

s.dp: Status › Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of στεφανόω ‘to crown’ or ‘to put a victory wreath on,’ not occurring in the NT with this meaning) to show particular honor to a person as the result of some type of victory

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: the trunk of the body from the neck to the abdomen

s.dp: Stances and Events Related to Stances › Stand
s.d: to be in a standing position{N:001}
to continue in a state, with a possible implication of acceptability
s.g: to continue to be; to stand
s.c: For a discussion of στήκω as part of an idiom in ⟦Romans 14:4|Romans 14:4⟧, see LN 87.56.

s.dp: Status › High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to his own master he stands or falls, probably a familiar adage) whether one maintains one’s status or relationship to a master depends on the masters judgment or evaluation
s.g: honor or disgrace depends on the person whom one serves

s.dp: Danger, Risk, Safe, Save › Safe, Free from Danger
s.d: a state of security and safety
s.g: place of safety; position of safety
s.c: For another interpretation of στηριγμός in ⟦2 Peter 3:17|2 Peter 3:17⟧, see LN 74.20.

s.d: a state of firm, inner strength
s.g: firm position; being firm in; firmness; steadfastness
s.c: For another interpretation of στηριγμός in ⟦2 Peter 3:17|2 Peter 3:17⟧, see LN 21.13.

s.d: to cause someone to become stronger in the sense of more firm and unchanging in attitude or belief
s.g: to strengthen; to make more firm

s.d: to put or place something firmly in a location
s.g: to cause to be fixed; to establish in a place

s.d: (a Semitic idiom, literally: to fix one’s face) to make a decision, with emphasis upon finality
s.g: to decide firmly; to resolve; to make up one’s mind definitely
s.c: In order to express the meaning of ‘to decide firmly,’ it may be useful in some instances to translate ‘to decide and to refuse to change one’s mind’ or ‘to decide and not to change.’

s.d: secondary projection from the trunk or bough of a tree or shrub, with its leaves attached

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: a permanent mark or scar on the body, especially the type of brand used to mark ownership of slaves{N:001}
s.c: In ⟦Galatians 6:17|Galatians 6:17⟧ Paul is most likely alluding to scars resulting from wounds received in the service of Jesus, but στίγμα may also imply ownership and hence suggest that such scars served as brands (see LN 8.56). For other interpretations of στίγμα in ⟦Galatians 6:17|Galatians 6:17⟧, see LN 33.481 and LN 90.84.

s.d: something on the surface of an object, for example, line, spot, or scar, without special design but carrying significance{N:002}
s.c: A strictly literal translation of ⟦Galatians 6:17|Galatians 6:17⟧ might suggest that Paul had the same marks on his hands, feet, and side as Jesus had, but this is evidently not the meaning of the state ment in ⟦Galatians 6:17|Galatians 6:17⟧. It is possible, of course, that since Paul was whipped much the same way that Jesus was whipped, he (Paul) would bear such scars on his back, but a more satisfactory rendering of ⟦Galatians 6:17|Galatians 6:17⟧ would probably be ‘for I have on my body scars indicating that I belong to Jesus.’ For other interpretations of στίγμα in ⟦Galatians 6:17|Galatians 6:17⟧, see LN 8.55 and LN 90.84.

s.dp: Time › Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
s.d: an extremely short unit of time
to give off or to reflect a very bright light
s.g: to glisten; to dazzle; to gleam; to flash

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: a covered colonnade, open normally on one side, where people could stand, sit, or walk, protected from the weather and the heat of the sun
s.c: Also see comments at LN 7.58.|In many parts of the world the closest equivalent to a στοά would be a veranda, an extensive type of porch. Such a porch may be described as ‘a long outside room’ or ‘a room made with pillars and open.’

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Philosophical
s.d: pertaining to the philosophical system of the Greek philosopher Zeno, who taught that people should be free from excessive joy or grief and submit without complaint to necessity
s.g: Stoic; one who adheres to Stoic philosophy
s.c: For comments on some translational problems, see LN 11.96.

s.d: the materials of which the world and the universe are composed
s.c: In many languages the closest equivalent of στοιχεῖα is ‘the things of which the world is made’ or ‘what the world is made of’ or ‘the substances of which the universe consists.’

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Powers
s.d: the supernatural powers or forces regarded as having control over the events of this world
s.g: the supernatural powers over this world
s.c: In a number of languages there is no way of speaking of ‘supernatural powers’ or ‘supernatural forces.’ Reference can only be made to such powers in terms of kinds of spirit beings; therefore, one may render στοιχεῖα in ⟦Colossians 2:20|Colossians 2:20⟧ as ‘those spirits that have power’ or ‘those spirits which control.’

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Basic Principles or Features Defining the Nature of Something
s.d: basic principles which underlie the nature of something
s.c: In some languages it may be extremely difficult to find the lexical equivalents of ‘the basic principles about the elementary aspects.’ In Greek this represents highly generic vocabulary, and in many languages the closest equivalent is ‘how to understand the simple truths.’ Therefore, this expression in ⟦Hebrews 5:12|Hebrews 5:12⟧ may be rendered as ‘again you have need for someone to teach you how to understand the simple truths about God’s message.’

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Behavior, Conduct
s.d: to live in conformity with some presumed standard or set of customs
s.g: to live; to behave in accordance with
s.c: In some languages it may be useful to restructure the relationships expressed by the reference to ‘the Spirit,’ and therefore one may translate this clause in ⟦Galatians 5:25|Galatians 5:25⟧ as ‘since the Spirit has given us life, we should also let him control our lives.’

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Imitate Behavior
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to follow in the tracks) to behave in the same manner as someone else
s.g: to imitate; to do as others do

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: a long, flowing robe
s.c: The cultural significance of ‘long robe’ would be high social status and dignified occupation or activity.

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.c: In some languages a distinction is made between terms used for the mouth when it is open and when it is closed. In ⟦Acts 23:2|Acts 23:2⟧ presumably the mouth was closed.|The term στόμα also occurs in a number of phrases associated with speech, but while in some languages one can say ‘to speak with the mouth,’ it may be more appropriate to say ‘to speak with the lips’ or ‘to speak with the tongue.’ In a number of contexts, however, it may be better simply to say ‘to speak,’ since the addition of ‘with the lips’ or ‘with the tongue’ or ‘with the mouth’ may appear to be unnecessarily redundant.

s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:στόμα<SDBG:στόμα:000000>}[a] ‘mouth,’ {D:8.19}) to communicate orally
(figurative extension of meaning of {L:στόμα<SDBG:στόμα:000000>}[a] ‘mouth,’ {D:8.19}) the faculty or capacity for speech
s.c: In ⟦Luke 1:64|Luke 1:64⟧ στόμα and γλῶσσα appear to have the same referent and therefore may be regarded as essentially synonymous.

s.d: that which has been spoken or uttered
(a figurative extension of meaning of {L:στόμα<SDBG:στόμα:000000>}[a] ‘mouth,’ {D:8.19}) the sharp edge of a weapon
s.c: For a discussion of στόμα μαχαίρης, see LN 6.33.

s.dp: Spacial Positions › In Front Of, Face To Face, In Back Of, Behind
s.d: (an idiom, literally: mouth to mouth) the position of persons facing one another and engaged in discussion
s.g: face to face; person to person

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to open the mouth to) to speak the complete truth to someone
s.g: to be completely open with; to conceal nothing from; to speak the whole truth to

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to block the mouth) to cause someone not to have anything to say
s.g: to silence; to remove any reason to speak

s.dp: Violence, Harm, Destroy, Kill › Harm, Wound
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to shut the mouth) to prevent harm or injury being done (in the one context in the NT, {S:05801103300022}, a reference to lions)
s.g: to stop the mouth of; to keep from harming
s.c: The particular historical reference of this phrase in ⟦Hebrews 11:33|Hebrews 11:33⟧ is not clear. In the account in ⟦Daniel 6:22|Daniel 6:22⟧ it is the angel of God which shut the mouths of the lions.

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: the upper part of the digestive tract, especially the stomach
s.c: In ⟦1 Timothy 5:23|1 Timothy 5:23⟧ it may be useful in some languages to translate ‘a little wine for the sake of your digestion’ or ‘… in order to help your digestion.’

s.d: act of engaging in war or battle as a soldier
s.c: στρατεύω and στρατεία in ⟦1 Timothy 1:18|1 Timothy 1:18⟧ and ⟦2 Corinthians 10:4|2 Corinthians 10:4⟧ are used figuratively, and it may be essential to mark this figurative usage as a type of simile. For example, in ⟦1 Timothy 1:18|1 Timothy 1:18⟧ στρατεύομαι may be rendered as ‘you may, so to speak, wage the good battle’ or ‘it is like you are fighting.’ Similarly, in ⟦2 Corinthians 10:4|2 Corinthians 10:4⟧ στρατεία may be rendered as ‘in what is like a battle for us.’

s.d: a large organized group of soldiers
a small detachment of soldiers
s.g: some soldiers; a few soldiers; a small group of soldiers

s.d: to engage in war or battle as a soldier
s.g: to battle; to fight; to engage in war; warfare
s.c: στρατεύω and στρατεία in ⟦1 Timothy 1:18|1 Timothy 1:18⟧ and ⟦2 Corinthians 10:4|2 Corinthians 10:4⟧ are used figuratively, and it may be essential to mark this figurative usage as a type of simile. For example, in ⟦1 Timothy 1:18|1 Timothy 1:18⟧ στρατεύομαι may be rendered as ‘you may, so to speak, wage the good battle’ or ‘it is like you are fighting.’ Similarly, in ⟦2 Corinthians 10:4|2 Corinthians 10:4⟧ στρατεία may be rendered as ‘in what is like a battle for us.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:στρατιώτης<SDBG:στρατιώτης:000000>} ‘soldier,’ {D:55.17}) to engage in military activity as a soldier
s.g: to serve as a soldier; to be a soldier

s.d: the chief legal official of a city
s.c: In a number of instances στρατηγός may be rendered simply as ‘the chief of the town’ or ‘the ruler of the city.’

s.d: (a title, literally: official of the temple) a commander of Jewish soldiers responsible for guarding and maintaining order in the Jewish Temple

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: (an idiom, literally: heavenly army) a large group or throng of angels
s.g: throng of angels; ranks of angels
s.c: There may be distinct objections to speaking of στρατιὰ οὐράνιος as being a ‘heavenly army,’ though undoubtedly in earlier times the thought of angels being God’s military force would have been quite appropriate. Therefore, in place of some expression which may refer to an army or military unit, it may be possible to translate στρατιὰ οὐράνιος as simply ‘many, many angels’ or ‘row after row of angels.’

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Powers
s.d: (an idiom, literally: army of heaven) the stars of heaven as symbols of various supernatural powers
s.c: Since ‘the stars of heaven’ serve primarily as symbols of certain heavenly supernatural powers, it may be appropriate in some languages to speak of ‘the spirits of the stars in the sky.’ See also LN 1.5.

s.d: a person of ordinary rank in an army
s.c: In some languages the normal equivalent of στρατιώτης would be ‘one who carries a gun,’ but such an expression would be completely anachronistic. Some translators have attempted to substitute a phrase such as ‘one who carries a sword,’ but this has failed in most cases since it suggests merely individual violence instead of organized warfare. It may therefore be important to use a phrase such as ‘one who fights under command’ or ‘one who is charged by the rulers to fight.’

s.d: to cause someone to be a soldier
s.c: In some languages it may be necessary to specify somewhat more clearly the relationship involved in ‘to enlist soldiers.’ For example, the last part of ⟦2 Timothy 2:4|2 Timothy 2:4⟧ may be rendered as ‘because he must please the one who caused him to be a soldier’ or ‘… who got him to be a soldier’ or ‘… who induced him to be a soldier for him.’ For another interpretation of στρατολογέω in ⟦2 Timothy 2:4|2 Timothy 2:4⟧, see LN 55.20.

s.d: to be a commanding officer of a group of soldiers
s.g: to be an army commander; to be an army officer

It is therefore essential in rendering these terms not to narrow the meaning too much, for in this way one would certainly do violence to certain crucial semantic features.|For another interpretation of στρέφομαι in ⟦Matthew 18:3|Matthew 18:3⟧, see LN 41.50.
